As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures believed that the sky was a dome above the Earth, and that the stars and planets were gods or spirits.

The ancient Greeks, in particular, were fascinated by the night sky and made detailed observations of the stars and constellations. They believed that the stars were fixed in place and that the Earth was a sphere, which was a revolutionary idea at the time.

The concept of a void of darkness in outer space, illuminated only by stars and galaxies, is a more modern idea that developed with the advent of modern astronomy in the 16th century. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model of the universe, which placed the Sun at the center of the solar system and the Earth and other planets in orbit around it.

The idea that space outside of Earth's atmosphere was blue as the morning sky is a myth that has been debunked by scientists. The color of space is actually black, as it absorbs all wavelengths of visible light. The blue color of the sky is an optical illusion caused by the scattering of sunlight by the Earth's atmosphere.

The first humans to observe the universe in detail were likely the ancient Chinese astronomers, who made detailed observations of the stars and planets using sophisticated astronomical instruments. The Chinese also developed a system of astronomy that included the concept of a void of darkness in outer space, which was later adopted by other cultures.

Overall, while humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years, our understanding of the universe has evolved significantly over time, and we have come to realize that space is a vast, dark, and mysterious void that is filled with stars, galaxies, and other celestial objects.
